Question 1

Which one of the following is a classic cluster sentence trick?

Correct!
A

Combining at least three forms of punctuation to make the structure more complex.

B

Separating the main noun from its verb.

Cluster sentences separate the main noun from its verb, like so:

Having just stepped off the plane in Ecuador, Ginny, who had just recently quit her job, a position at a law firm filled with drama, some of which was entirely preventable, expected a quiet vacation but instead found herself face to face with a hurricane.

C

Combining abstract language with technical jargon.

initial.html:
Question 2

To separate the main noun from its verb, cluster sentences often use a ton of commas:

Having just stepped off the plane in Ecuador , Ginny , who had just recently quit her job , a position at a law firm filled with drama , some of which was entirely preventable , expected a quiet vacation but instead found herself face to face with a hurricane.

But this is actually a blessing! Check out our Ginny sentence without commas:

Having just stepped off the plane in Ecuador Ginny who had just recently quit her job a position at a law firm filled with drama some of which was entirely preventable expected a quiet vacation but instead found herself face to face with a hurricane.

Question 7

Using middle-out, let's identify which parts of the following sentence are core elements and which parts are optional elements.

The book, which was a gift, sat on the shelf.

Is "which was a gift" an optional element or a core element?

Correct! You got it right on the first try!

When you have two or more commas in a sentence, use middle-out. If the middle piece of the sentence can be a complete thought by itself, both outer pieces are optional. If the middle piece can’t be a complete thought, it's an optional element.
